page: Google Cloud Platform c4-highmem-4-lssd is an x86_64 architecture server powered by a dedicated Intel Xeon 6985P-C processor. It features 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, running at a base clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The system is equipped with 31.0 GB of RAM, yielding 7.75 GB per core, and includes a bundled 137 GB local NVMe SSD for high-speed storage.

Benchmark results indicate a mix of capabilities. Single-core performance is generally average, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2240.59 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1858.0. However, multi-core performance is weaker, as evidenced by a stress-ng multi-core score of 4549.86 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 4215.0. Memory bandwidth is a notable bottleneck, with large-block read bandwidth registering at a poor 22.46 GB/sec and write bandwidth at a weak 15.13 GB/sec. Conversely, the server excels in single-threaded text processing, achieving a top-tier Geekbench score of 2828.0, and single-threaded gzip compression, which is strong at 35.55 GB/sec.

Given its high memory-to-vCPU ratio and local NVMe SSD, this instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound workloads that do not require massive parallel processing. It is well-suited for single-threaded text processing, lightweight database operations, caching layers like Redis (achieving 7.38 million SET operations per second), and small-scale LLM inference, where it processes 135M model prompts at an average of 591.08 tokens per second. It is less optimal for heavy multi-threaded computing or high-throughput memory-intensive applications due to its constrained multi-core performance and memory bandwidth.

While its single-core CPU performance and single-threaded operations like text processing and gzip compression are average to strong, its multi-core scaling and memory bandwidth are relatively weak. Specifically, large-block read memory bandwidth is limited to 22.46 GB/sec. This hardware profile makes the server qualitatively cost-effective for memory-intensive, single-threaded tasks, Redis caching, and lightweight database operations rather than highly parallelized compute workloads.
